prompt: An external sort has produced 1,024 sorted runs on disk, holding one billion records in total. Which way of producing the final sorted output does the least comparison work, and why?

options.text: Concatenate the runs and sort everything again, because comparison sorting is the optimal way to order records
options.explanation: A full re-sort throws away the order the runs already have. Each record would cost about 30 comparison levels (the base-2 logarithm of a billion) instead of about 10.

options.text: For each output record, scan the heads of all 1,024 runs and take the smallest
options.explanation: This is correct but slow: about 1,024 comparisons per record, roughly a hundred times the heap merge's cost.

options.text: Keep a min-heap of the 1,024 run heads; pop the smallest and push the next record from the same run
options.explanation: Correct. The heap never holds more than 1,024 items, so each record costs one pop and one push through about 10 heap levels (the base-2 logarithm of 1,024). That is around ten comparison steps per record, up to a small constant.

options.text: Merge run 1 with run 2, then the result with run 3, and so on up to run 1,024
options.explanation: Records from the first runs are re-read and re-copied in almost every one of the 1,023 merges, so total work grows with the number of records times the number of runs.
